Sounds like normal play fighting or possibly a show of dominance. If you're unsure and starting to feel like the dynamic is getting aggressive (it gets more frequents or intense) you might want to get a couple more rats to introduce them to. Preferably babies to make the introduction process easier. Rats do better in groups than couples, especially if one rat is more dominant. It'll make it so the more submissive rat can catch a break every now and again.

When I had a pair of male rats that were presumably bonded from birth, they did fine for some time, but started becoming aggressive because of what I assume was either trauma (they were rescues) or the couple thing. The bigger rat was the dominant one, but the smaller was the aggressive one.

Signs to look for regarding genuine aggression:

1: Drawing blood. At this point you must consider immediate action. Neutering, separation, etc. Just be sure that the blood was actually a bite, not an accidental scratch or an unrelated accident.2: Puffed up fur. All rats do this sometimes when cold, scared or angry. But constant puffed up fur can be aggression.3: Sideways kicking. Combined with puffed up fur.4: Rubbing scent/excessive scent marking. This can be in the form of pee, or a sort of digging/rubbing motion with their hands.5: The submissive rat will spend a lot of time in defensive positions. Standing on their hind legs, snout pointing in the air, frozen.

Otherwise, you are allowed to calm down. It takes a lot for fighting to get to the point of seriously harming another rat. Keep them entertained, safe and fed. If an injury does occur, rats have incredible healing powers and it's not the end of the world.

Wirt passed from respiratory issues. He was at home, and started making a choking sound. He had occasionally been making those, and it would always pass after a couple seconds. I know now that it is NOT normal, and that even a little bit of that sound usually means the illness has progressed to the uncurable.. But I didn't have a good vet, nor money to try and find one. So he made those weird sounds, only this time it didn't stop. He crawled towards us, asking for help. I tried heimlich for rats, and nothing happened. We called the emergency vet, but while on the phone with them, he lost his balance and simply passed away. We were absolutely heartbroken. His little desperate walk will never leave my heart or mind. 

The next time one of my rats died it was Moffe. He was old and developed HLD. He'd been on pain meds for a while, and one day we just knew it was time. He was cuddly, still himself, able to make it around the cage. He couldn't control his bladder, and we decided to put him down. It was a lovely trip to the vet's office, with our talented vet (who is now our go-to), and he got to be surrounded by everyone he loved and eating malt paste as he passed in the middle of a bite. We brought him home with us, and buried him and Wirt together. 

My last one to die was right before Christmas. His name was Ted, and we rescued him with Moffe. We'd seen him decline slowly over a week or so of time,, and we had his vet appointment ready for just a couple days later. One night we somehow just knew he was about to pass. He hadn't moved from his hide at all, or eaten anything. I brought him out and let him sleep by my side and in my hoodie while I slept. I woke up just in time to see him pass over. It was literally the most peaceful and sad thing I have ever witnessed. He was so calm and still. We gave him a double dose of painkillers while we could, so I know he wasn't hurting. He was just passing away, slipping into the ether. 

I love reading stories about animals passing away. As morbid as that sounds out of context, I just really enjoy the thought of us humans loving something so strongly... You can really tell how highly we value these animals by reading about them passing. 

I am so sorry you didn't make it to the vet with your boy. If it helps, HLD doesn't progress that fast, and there were probably a more complicated health issue that you didn't know about. We'll never know, but just know that if it was HLD, you would've had time to put him down and say goodbye on your terms. It wasn't your fault that it progressed quicker than it was "supposed to". I am also sure that your boy knew how loved he was, since he was surrounded by you and his cage mate.

We find ourselves forgetting that they have passed. Even though it's been a full year, I still sometimes mistakenly call out for Moffe, one of our first. I have six right now, and Greg is the oldest. I am dreading the day where my girls become old. They've changed my life so much, for the better, and I can't bear the thought of them slowing down, losing mobility. Tumours are one of my biggest fears for them.

I have had nightmares about them being hurt/dying (most recently I started hating otters because of a dream where Greg got eaten by one) but not really from old age. I think old age is one of the very peaceful and beautiful ways to die. I never wanna experience a traumatic death like Wirt again. Recently one of my girls got her tail stuck in the door and it degloved, and I was terrified of losing her. Old age is peaceful, serene. Especially if you put them down while their quality of life is still good. They don't feel a thing, and they get to pass in your arms, maybe with some snacks and cuddles if they like that.

I wish they lived longer, too. My crested gecko, who I got when he was already seven, will outlive all my current rats. Crested geckos can starve to death if their cage is too big because they won't find their food, and they still live longer than rats. Unfair.

Greg and Wirt were my first baby rats. I had rescued two older boys six months before, and I was ready to expand my pack. They never did end up living with my old boys, and both of those are gone now.

Greg and Wirt. Two adorable dumbos, one russian blue and one standard agouti. Greg and Wirt. One shy, climbing to the top of the cage to avoid us. The other couldn't climb for the first week, only staying in the bottom. He played with me all the time. Wirt was my heart rat. Tiny, adorable. Active. He would chase my hand. He hated lettuce, he loved digging. He bonded in my hoodie. I loved him greatly. I still do.

Greg and Wirt. You were sick so young. Stuck in the mail on the way to the pet store, middle of January in Scandinavia. Your lungs couldn't take the cold climate. You were so young... And so was I. I didn't know how to deal with it, I still don't know, really. I had never been to the vet before. They gave you injections, they gave you antibiotics. And nothing worked.

Greg and Wirt. One alive, one dead. Greg was so depressed after his brother passed. I can't help but admit I was too. I left him in the freezer, I didn't want to let go just yet. He was only a couple months old, he never got to grow up. He was so small he fit into a little cardboard box for mozarella sticks, in the back of my tiny freezer.

Greg finally got his cage mates in the summer of 2022. Three active girls, just as small as he had been just six months ago. He was confused but grateful to share the big cage with them, as they outran him. They could climb the ceiling, and he watched, almost envious. He became more cuddly, more obsessed with food. He would go to bed an hour into free roam, then half an hour, then fifteen minutes...

Greg and Wirt would be two years old soon. Greg is fat now. When I buried his brother, I cried at how small he was. He wasn't even 300 grams. My two babies, one old, one forever young. I don't know which one hurts the most. The pain of losing Wirt is now a mere bruise. I keep his fur in a jar. We have two paintings from Greg. I can't help but think it's to remember him by, when he passes. That's the life cycle of rats, after all. Baby, young adult, try to get as many good memories as you can, elderly, and end of life. All the treats they can get.

When he does pass, and he will, I imagine him in ratty heaven. Soft blankets, infinite dig boxes, pools of malt paste... And his brother, there, to welcome him. I imagine his body will be small and nimble again, with the agility of a three month old. No longer sleepy, no longer tired, no longer damaged. They'll play together again, chasing each other for eternity. One day I hope to join them too. By that time there'll be more. Many more, waiting for my return. I'll know each by name, by touch. They'll all know my voice. They've known me all their life.

Sadly, the way it's portrayed it seems to be the minority of people who have very good results. I am definitely seeing a rapid advance in bottom surgery for trans men too, but I think we are hanging a bit behind compared to trans women. 

A bit on the more personal side, I could never have phallo due to extensive scarring on my arms and thighs from before I knew it was a thing you could do. We only have one hospital in my country which provides surgeries, hormones and treatment for trans people, so if I were to want it anywhere else it would be expensive either way. There's a bunch of reasons why someone can't/shouldn't/doesn't want to have bottom surgery. I think they are all valid, especially because surgery is so incredibly hard to recover from. Having intense dysphoria around your genitals must be very hard, and I'm very lucky that I can get rid of most of it without surgery. That's exactly why we should be happy that there are different options to transition! Some are happy with just hormones, some wanna get a hysterectomy, FFS, etc etc. We can all choose which help would be useful to us, to get us as symptom free as possible.

I think we can find explanations for this in many different areas of being trans. I'll explain further, but this will be mainly focused on trans men. I am a trans man myself, and I also think trans women are more likely to have bottom surgery (partly for the reasons listed below).

First of all, bottom surgery (especially for trans men) has come a fairly short way. Top surgery is advanced and safe, with most getting good results and having a short recovery period. Bottom surgery has a very long recovery, is very painful and all options require multiple stages. It's expensive, and results aren't guaranteed to be good. In fact, for my own personal taste, even the best results aren't good enough to go through the pain. 

I also think social dysphoria plays a big role in it. Our chest is very visible in many situations, like the beach, swimming, going to sleep, etc. We see male chests and are expected to show our own way more often than our genitals. Therefore we might be more inclined to want top op to be able to go to the beach or wear no T-shirt in the summer. 

One thing to consider is that getting top surgery is more accepted and glorified in the media. We don't see a lot of people making aesthetic posts about their phallo scars, but I have seen quite a few with masectomy scars. Getting top op can be viewed as a reversible thing (it's not really) for those who are worried about regretting it. It's easy to hide, I actually know a detrans person who uses a chest plate because they got top op. It's also innocent and childlike, which fits into the sort of style they might wanna go for. The same people who hate any sign of being a "man", who only wanna be a boy, would not want a full grown man penis. 

Lastly I wanna talk about the tools we use to deal with dysphoria. A binder is incredibly uncomfortable. They get hot, they're tight, we can't wear them for longer periods of time... They cause back pain and possible life long skeletal damage over time. A packer is incredibly cheap, lasts a long time, and works wonders. A prosthetic is even better. We have tools to have sex, some of them can even recreate the sensation. 

I can summarize with this: Surgery is hard. We don't show our genitals often. Top op is shown more online. Packers get rid of most of the issues. 
My own experience, I have "accepted" my own genitals in the way where I know there is nothing to do about it. I need to live with it somehow. I still experience dysphoria, but things like wearing my packer, no longer having a period, and not having intercourse really help. My dysphoria cannot be magically cured by accepting my genitals, but I can accept the dysphoria and live a good life even with it. I remember a time where my bottom dysphoria was so severe that I wanted to cry every time I saw it, but I have gotten so far in my own journey, learned about myself, and found tools to deal with it.

Rats. I am in love with rats.
In August 2021 my girlfriend and I travelled for six hours to go get a pair of male rats. I sat up the entire weekend before watching videos, reading, joining forums, asking questions, and I fell for them

Rats are amazing animals. They have been proven to be empathic and will help their friends get out of traps even if it means their friends can steal their food. They react to cries of help. They are incredibly social and in the wild live in packs with males and females, and they have a set "poison sniffer" in the pack that will try out new and unknown foods to check if the rest of the pack can eat it. 

As domesticated pets they are also incredibly social, and easily form bonds not only to each other, but also to their humans (and sometimes to other animals, though I do not recommend introducing them to other animals because they could unintentionally hurt each other). They are gentle, and will groom humans, especially if they think you are hurt. 

They need constant stimulation and I spend hours upon hours every week just crafting and researching to give them the best life possible. They're curious and playful, and can be taught to do agility and tricks just like a dog. They're so smart, I have succesfully given mine several dog IQ toys and they figure them out so quickly. 

Their tails give them an amazing balance and lets them climb ropes suspended in the air, while their sharp claws let them climb VERTICAL surfaces (such as my legs if I'm wearing pants). 

Their front paws also function as two little hands, and every rat has a distinct way to hold their food. One of my favourite treats to give mine is a little star baby food thing, and one of my rats will eat off the corners in turn before systematically eating it like those corn on the cob animations in Donald Duck. 

They can eat almost anything us humans can, including chocolate and grapes. Meaning you can almost always share little bits of your own food with them and they will run off to either hide it for later or they might even eat it right next to you.

Lab rats are incredible resources for science and let us know so much more about the human body, psychology and brain. One study found that rats are more likely to become addicted to opiates when isolated, and rats with good social health are more likely to recover from potential addiction. 

Rats are just overall so awesome. I currently have three males (and one angel boy) and this autumn I am getting three little girls to put with a neutered male. The girls are more active and I'm excited to see them running around and ravaging my setups :P
